BOTTOM LINE. The paper is real, is in a top-3 journal, and its core quarterly association is more robust than I expected. But the two things the article actually wants to lean on — the 29% cumulative figure and the top-10-led size gradient — are the two least-vetted, least-identified objects in the paper. The 29% in particular fails on four independent grounds and must not carry weight. Full findings below, organized by attack surface.

=== 1. IDENTIFICATION: there is none, and the paper never claims otherwise until it does ===
Table 6.2 is a contemporaneous OLS time-series regression: quarterly excess return of the top-N portfolio over the S&P500, regressed on the same quarter's change in S&P500 index-fund ownership share. No instrument, no event study, no discontinuity, no difference-in-differences. I grepped the entire manuscript: the words "endogeneity," "reverse causality," "instrument," and "identification strategy" appear NOWHERE in the empirical section (the only hits for "identify"/"exogenous" are in the theory's algebra and one appendix sentence). The regression body correctly uses associational language throughout ("is associated with"). Then on p.36 the paper switches registers without warrant: "the rise in passive investing over the past 25 years CAUSED a firm that was in the top 50 ... to rise by 29% more than the index." That causal verb is not earned by anything in Section 6.

Reverse causality is not hypothetical here. PassiveFlow is net dollar flow into SPY/IVV/VOO + ICI S&P500 index mutual funds, scaled by index cap. Index-fund and ETF net flows are strongly performance-chasing at quarterly frequency. Controls include the contemporaneous and lagged S&P500 return, which absorbs the linear level-chasing channel — but the object at risk is precisely the nonlinear one: megacap-led rallies are the salient, headline-generating rallies that pull retail and 401(k) money into index products. A linear R_SP500 control cannot absorb "flows respond more strongly when the rally is led by the largest names," which is exactly the confound that would generate this coefficient with zero price impact.

DECISIVE TEST THE PAPER DECLINES TO RUN: there is no lagged-flow → return regression anywhere in the paper or its appendices. Not one. This is a two-line Stata change on a dataset they already have, and it is the natural test of whether flows PRECEDE the relative price move. Its absence is conspicuous. And note what happens in the one specification where they DO impose temporal ordering (Table 6.3, idiosyncratic volatility on one-quarter-lagged flow): the direct effect of lagged PassiveFlow is 20.63 with t = 1.21 — insignificant. Only the Top50 interaction survives (19.32, t = 2.53). So the single place in the paper where flows are dated before outcomes, the main effect vanishes.

=== 2. THE 29% IS ARITHMETIC, NOT AN ESTIMATE — and it is the article's weakest available number ===
The construction (p.36) is 0.528% × (0.05/0.09) × 99 = 29.04%. Algebraically this is just β_raw × cumulative flow, i.e. 5.87% of relative outperformance per 1 percentage point of index-fund ownership share, applied to the 4.95pp cumulative share increase. Four separate failures:

(a) FREQUENCY MISMATCH — the fatal one. The coefficient is identified off quarter-to-quarter deviations in the flow series (SD 0.09pp). The 29% applies that coefficient to the series' DRIFT term (mean 0.05pp/qtr), cumulated 99 times. These are different sources of variation. The regression contains no information about the low-frequency trend relationship; that variation is soaked up by the constant. The extrapolation projects a high-frequency slope 55 standard deviations out of sample (4.95pp / 0.09pp = 55 SDs) with no functional-form evidence whatsoever. Over 1996–2020 both the passive share and megacap concentration trended upward; the 29% is, structurally, a trend-on-trend attribution dressed as a regression result.

(b) THE AUTHORS' OWN MODEL REJECTS IT. Their calibrated structural model (Tables 5.2–5.5) produces a top-group premium of 0% (pure active-to-passive switch, full index — Table 5.2) up to ~4% (Table 5.5, partial large-stock index with noise traders). The paper states this plainly on p.36 and offers two unquantified excuses (fewer truly active investors than calibrated; partial mean-reversion). So the paper contains an unresolved internal inconsistency of a factor of 7 to infinity between its reduced form and the structural model the same authors built and calibrated to match empirical moments. An article that cites 29% is citing the number the paper's own theory cannot generate.

(c) NO STANDARD ERROR IS EVER REPORTED ON IT, and mean-reversion — the authors' own stated caveat — is never estimated despite being trivially testable (regress k-quarter-ahead cumulative excess returns on flow). Propagating only the coefficient's sampling error (t = 3.66 ⇒ SE ≈ 0.144), the 95% CI on 29.04% is roughly [13.5%, 44.6%]. That understates true uncertainty badly, since extrapolation and mean-reversion risk are the dominant terms and are unquantified.

(d) IT IS AN ARTIFACT OF THE top-50 CUT. Running the same cumulation on the paper's other four portfolios: top-10 → 37.8% [7.7%, 67.9%]; top-100 → 16.7%; top-150 → 11.4%; top-200 → 8.0% [−1.6%, 17.5%], insignificant. The "cumulative effect of passive on megacaps" therefore ranges from statistically zero to 68% depending on which arbitrary top-N line you draw. "29%" is not a finding; it is one point on a continuum, selected by reporting convention.

=== 3. VERSION DRIFT — the two load-bearing numbers are ~1 year old and were never seminar-tested ===
This is the finding I did not expect and it is important for the article's "best-credentialed" framing. I diffed three versions:
• NBER w28253 rev.1, Sept 2022 (Table 8): ONE large portfolio only (top 50, confirmed via matching descriptives: mean −0.15/−0.17, SD 1.56/1.86). No top-10/100/150/200 gradient. No cumulative extrapolation — grep for "Cumulating"/"cumulative effect" returns nothing.
• LSE FMG DP868-revised, April 2024: same. Still no gradient table, still no 29%.
• RFS accepted version, June 2025: Panel B (the five-portfolio monotone gradient, top-10 = 0.687%) and the 29% cumulation both appear for the first time.
Both therefore entered between April 2024 and June 2025, in the final RFS revision round(s), on a dataset frozen at 2020Q4. The paper's extensive vetting record — AFA, CICF, FIRS, Q-Group, Adam Smith Asset Pricing, BIS, LSE, and roughly a dozen seminars listed in the acknowledgments — is vetting of versions that did NOT contain either number. The credentialing the article is implicitly invoking does not extend to the specific figures it wants to quote.
Credit where due, and this matters: the top-50 quarterly coefficient is remarkably stable across the three versions (0.00549/0.00550/0.00523/0.00525 in 2022 and 2024 → 0.00557/0.00553/0.00531/0.00528 in 2025). That number has a genuine track record. The gradient and the 29% do not.

=== 4. SAMPLE AND WINDOW — the Mag-7 era is entirely out of sample ===
1996Q2–2020Q4, N = 99 quarterly aggregate observations. The sample end date is identical in the December 2020 first draft and the June 2025 accepted version: across 4.5 years of revision, roughly 18 additional quarters became available and none were added. Those 18 quarters (2021Q1–2025Q1) are precisely the period of the concentration surge the article wants to explain. "Magnificent Seven" is a 2023 coinage. The paper's in-sample concentration episodes are the dot-com run-up and the 2015–2020 FAANG run; it contains zero observations of the 2023–2025 concentration peak. I have no evidence the result would fail out of sample — but the article cannot represent this paper as evidence ABOUT the Mag 7. It is evidence about an earlier era, offered as a mechanism that might extend.
Additional sample concerns: the regressor has excess kurtosis 3.62 on N = 99, so a handful of quarters (plausibly 2000Q1, 2008Q4, 2020Q1–Q2) likely dominate the fit. No winsorization, no influence diagnostics, no robust regression, no bootstrap — I grepped for all of these and found none. There is also NO subsample or subperiod split anywhere in the paper (no "subsample," "subperiod," "first half," "second half," or dot-com-exclusion test). For a 25-year time-series regression with 99 observations spanning two structurally different concentration regimes, the absence of any temporal stability check is a standard referee demand that appears not to have been made.

=== 5. INFERENCE — the gradient is asserted, never tested; R² is thin ===
Adjusted R² across Table 6.2 Panel B: 0.049 (top-10), 0.125, 0.105, 0.124, 0.125. SEs are Newey-West with 3 lags on 99 observations.
The headline top-10 column is the WEAKEST cell in the table on every dimension except point estimate: largest coefficient (0.687), lowest t (2.46), lowest adjusted R² (0.049), and the noisiest dependent variable (top-10 excess return SD = 3.86% quarterly vs 1.86% for top-50). That is the signature of a small, lumpy portfolio — over 1996–2020 the top 10 is a handful of names whose relative return is driven by a few firm-specific episodes. The top-200 endpoint is insignificant (0.145, t = 1.64, p ≈ 0.10 two-sided).
Critically: the paper NEVER TESTS THE GRADIENT. There is no reported test that β_top10 > β_top200, no interaction specification, no joint test of monotonicity. The "monotone decline" is read off five point estimates whose confidence intervals overlap heavily (top-10 CI [0.140, 1.234]; top-200 CI [−0.028, 0.318]). A naive difference test assuming independence gives t ≈ 1.85 (p ≈ 0.06); the true SE is smaller than that because the portfolios are nested and positively correlated, so the gradient is probably real — but "probably real, never tested" is not the same as "established," and the article should not describe monotonicity as a finding of the paper when the paper never estimated it.
Multiple testing: five overlapping portfolios × {value-, equal-weighted} × {with, without controls}, plus S&P600, plus three concentration measures, plus idio-vol, plus month-start, plus idiosyncratic beta. No multiplicity adjustment anywhere. The nesting means these are not independent tests, but it also means the reported headline (top-50) is the strongest-t cell of a family.

=== 6. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY — the measure is narrow, and its meaning drifts within the sample ===
PassiveFlow covers only S&P500-tracking index mutual funds (ICI) plus three ETFs (SPY, IVV, VOO). Cumulative change over 25 years: 4.95pp of index capitalization. Excluded: total-market and broad-index funds, Russell/CRSP trackers, target-date funds, institutional internal indexation, and closet indexing — all of which also buy megacaps proportionally, and the paper's own introduction concedes passive growth is "more than twice as high" once benchmark-hugging is counted.
The paper discloses (p.32) that S&P500 index mutual funds are "47% to 87% of the assets of all index mutual funds invested in US stocks in our sample." That range is a within-sample drift: the regressor covers most of index investing early and roughly half of it late. So the omitted passive complex is (i) growing, (ii) positively correlated with the included regressor, and (iii) in the error term. That is time-varying measurement error in the construct; Newey-West does not touch it.
This produces a REDUCTIO that the article should confront directly. If the linear cumulation is valid, then applying the same 5.87%-per-pp multiplier to the broader passive share the article actually cares about (the paper's own stated ~16% of the market, or ~20pp of growth) yields cumulative megacap outperformance north of 100%. That is absurd, which means the linearity assumption underlying the 29% is self-refuting at exactly the scope the article wants to use it. Conversely, if only the narrow S&P500-fund slice has this effect, then the mechanism does not generalize to "passive inflates the Mag 7." The article cannot have it both ways.
Separately on the multiplier: β_raw implies ~5.9% relative price impact per 1pp of ownership share, PERMANENTLY, on a CROSS-SECTIONAL (relative) price. Aggregate-market inelasticity multipliers in the Gabaix–Koijen tradition are of similar order, but relative prices within the S&P500 should be far MORE elastic than the aggregate, because relative-value arbitrage within a large-cap index is cheap, unlevered, and unconstrained compared with levering the whole market. A relative-price multiplier as large as the aggregate one is theoretically uncomfortable and the paper does not address it.

=== 7. THE ROBUSTNESS TESTS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT ===
The paper calls two appendix exercises corroboration of Table 6.2. Neither is.
(a) Table E.8 (concentration): same 99 quarters, same regressor, and a dependent variable — change in the log combined index weight of the top 10 firms — that is very nearly an algebraic transform of the top-10 excess return already in Table 6.2 Panel B (for a fixed constituent set, Δlog w_top10 ≈ log((1+r_top10)/(1+r_index))). This is a restatement, not a replication. Its t-stats without controls are also marginal: 2.30, 2.02, 1.92 (the HHI version is below 2).
(b) Table E.9 (month-start dummy): described as "a proxy to capture exogenous variation," it is never used as an instrument for PassiveFlow, so it contributes nothing to the 0.687/0.528 estimates. And it is confounded by the turn-of-the-month return effect — documented since Ariel (JFE 1987), Lakonishok & Smidt (RFS 1988), and Ogden (JF 1990) — a calendar anomaly that long predates meaningful index-fund flows and has at least four competing explanations (paycheck/pension flows, month-end window dressing, cash-flow settlement timing, clustered information release). The paper cannot separate its interpretation from those. Notably, this test's own gradient also dies early: t = 2.28 (top-10), 2.82, 2.10, then 1.07 (top-150) and 0.16 (top-200), on adjusted R² of 0.0066 across 2.97M daily observations.

=== 8. THE PLACEBO IS WEAK, AND ITS POINT ESTIMATE HAS THE WRONG SIGN ===
Table 6.4 (S&P600, N = 77): coefficients are −0.0054, −0.0054, −0.0040, −0.0039, all insignificant (t = −1.26 to −0.75). The paper reports this as "consistent with our model," invoking the auxiliary prediction that flows lift an index's largest members only when those are also the economy's largest. Two problems. First, the point estimates are NEGATIVE and of roughly the same absolute magnitude as the S&P500 top-50 effect — the placebo is not a null, it is a mirror image, which is what one would expect if the S&P500 result were partly a size/style factor rather than a flow effect. Second, power: the S&P600 top-60 excess return has SD 3.41–3.89% (vs 1.86% for S&P500 top-50) on 77 rather than 99 observations, so implied SEs are ~0.42–0.43. The specification can only marginally reject the S&P500 magnitude (+0.528 sits ~2.2–2.5 SE from the S&P600 point estimates). More fundamentally, the model's flexibility means the S&P600 result cannot discipline the S&P500 result: the theory accommodates a positive, null, or negative coefficient depending on which index is tested, so no S&P600 outcome would have falsified anything.

=== 9. AUTHOR INCENTIVES — disclosed, mild, worth one clause ===
The paper acknowledges financial support from the LSE Paul Woolley Centre. Vayanos directs that centre, whose formal name is the Paul Woolley Centre for the Study of Capital Market Dysfunctionality — an institution founded on the thesis that delegated and benchmarked investment management causes market dysfunction. The paper also cites Vayanos & Woolley (2013) as theoretical support for the month-start test. This is academic, disclosed, and not industry money, so I weight it lightly: it is a research-program prior, not a financial conflict, and it does not by itself discount any coefficient. It is relevant only because the article proposes to present the paper as neutral best-available evidence; a one-clause disclosure is proportionate. There is a strong counterweight in the authors' favor: they voluntarily flag their own 29%-vs-4% discrepancy on the same page they report it, which is exactly what good-faith reporting looks like. The integrity problem here is downstream — an article that quotes 29% WITHOUT the caveat the authors themselves attached misrepresents the paper more than the paper misrepresents itself.

=== WHAT SURVIVES ===
One thing, cleanly: over 1996Q2–2020Q4, quarters with higher net flows into S&P500 index funds were quarters in which the index's largest constituents outperformed the index, ~+0.5%/quarter per one-SD flow for the top 50, t ≈ 3.7, adjusted R² ~0.13, stable to three decimals across three paper versions spanning 2022–2025. That is a robust contemporaneous ASSOCIATION over a window ending in 2020. Everything the article wants beyond that — the causal verb, the megacap-tilted gradient, the 29%, and the extension to the Mag 7 — is either untested, unidentified, out of sample, or contradicted by the paper's own calibration.

Primary texts audited locally: /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/cs_jfe.txt (accepted MS dated April 7, 2024) and /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/cs_2022.txt (SSRN 4188052 working paper, July 19, 2022; earlier circulated as "Excess Reconstitution-Day Volume"). Bottom line: the paper is real, peer-reviewed, and its DIRECTIONAL claim survives. The specific figure 33.5% does not survive as a point estimate of "the true passive share," for six independent reasons, three of which I regard as disqualifying for load-bearing use.

=== FINDING 1 (disqualifying). The paper's central validation test has zero power against the only error that matters: level bias. ===
The identifying restriction is Eq. (8): for index i on recon day t, every addition and every deletion must imply the SAME AUM_indexed_i. The famous intro demonstration (YETI implies $5.3t; SUNRUN, with a different price $54.38 and weight 0.027%, "needed" 26.4m shares and printed 26.8m) and Table 5's "average absolute measurement error 1.00 (full sample)" are tests of PROPORTIONALITY — that recon-day volume scales as IndexWeight/Price across stocks in the same event. They are NOT tests of the level. If every recon-day print is a constant multiple k of true passive rebalancing need — because of two-sided crossing, liquidity-provider unwinds, derivative hedging, or ordinary trading that happens to scale with index weight — the test passes perfectly at any k, while AUM is overstated k-fold. The paper's own Table 4 proves the test has no power over k: five proxies for the same 2021 quantity give 33.50 / 28.65 / 24.62 / 22.53 / 13.31 — a 2.5x range — and nothing in the ±1% cross-validation discriminates among them. "There is very little left for active managers to explain" (p.6) is a non sequitur: the evidence shows volume is proportional to passive demand, not that it equals it.

=== FINDING 2 (disqualifying). The published design INCLUDES precisely the events the authors' own prior version EXCLUDED as uninterpretable — and those events supply ~61% of the headline. ===
The 2022 working paper, §3 (cs_2022.txt L397-408, L926-935): "the third Friday of March, June, September, and December are triple witching days when single-stock options, index options, and index futures all expire at the same time. On these days, there is high closing volume for reasons unrelated to any reconstitution events. This limits the number of benchmark indexes we can use... If a reconstitution event were to occur on a triple-witching day, we would not be able to distinguish end-of-day volume due to index reconstitutions from end-of-day volume due to derivatives trading. This is why we do not apply our approach to estimate the passive-ownership share of investors who are benchmarked to indexes, such as the Nasdaq 100, which reconstitute on triple-witching days... if we were to include these indexes in our analysis, we would tend to overstate the passive-ownership share." They enforced it: Table 1 of the 2022 draft drops witching-day S&P 500 events, "leaving 149 S&P 500 events in total," and drops the Nasdaq 100 entirely.
The JFE version silently reverses both exclusions. JFE L389: S&P 500 and MidCap 400 scheduled reconstitutions "take place on the third Friday of March, June, September, and December which represent triple-witching days." JFE L469: the Nasdaq 100 annual rebalance "lines up with the final witching day of the calendar year." Table 3 (2021): S&P 500 = 16.80pp, Nasdaq 100 = 3.76pp of the 33.50pp total — i.e. 20.56/33.50 = 61% of the headline comes from indexes whose reconstitutions sit on witching days that the same authors, two years earlier, said made the estimate uninterpretable and biased upward. The JFE paper never cites, retracts, or engages its own prior exclusion rule. Its own Figure 9 confirms the contaminant is material: the Friday-before-Russell triple-witching day lifts the closing-volume share of R2000 adds from 3.2% (normal) to 14.9% — a 4.7x elevation — on a day with NO index event.
The entire defense is two unsupported sentences: "We find similar point estimates for the total AUM indexed to the S&P 500 and MidCap 400 when using regularly scheduled and ad hoc changes" (L394) and the same for the Nasdaq 100 (L474). No table, no numbers, no standard errors, no appendix. The single most important robustness check in the paper — the one that reverses the authors' own earlier design decision — is asserted, not shown.

=== FINDING 3 (disqualifying). The most contaminated component fails an external level check by roughly 6-8x. ===
Backing out the denominator from the paper's own text ($15.1t passive AUM = 33.5% ⇒ TotalMarketCap 2021 ≈ $45.1t), Table 3's components imply: S&P 500 ≈ $7.6t (paper's own Figure A1 confirms $7.5t); Russell 1000 ≈ $4.9t; S&P MidCap ≈ $0.50t; Russell 2000 ≈ $0.48t; NASDAQ 100 ≈ $1.69t. The S&P 500 component reconciles well with S&P DJI's own indexed-assets survey (~$7.4t indexed to the S&P 500 at end-2021), so the estimator is roughly calibrated where witching contamination is diluted across quarterly + ad hoc events. The Nasdaq 100 component does not survive contact with reality: QQQ's net assets were $182.5bn at FY-end 2021 (Invesco QQQ Trust Series 1, SEC Form N-30B-2, FY2021); Nasdaq's own current "Nasdaq-100 ecosystem" tally is ~$1.4t TOTAL and that is split roughly 50/50 between funds (~$587bn in ETFs) and DERIVATIVES, measured four-plus years later. Chinco-Sammon's $1.69t of 2021 NDX-indexed AUM is thus (a) ~9x contemporaneous QQQ, (b) roughly 6x plausible total 2021 NDX fund assets, and (c) larger than the entire NDX fund complex today. It is, however, the right order of magnitude for the NDX fund-plus-derivatives complex — exactly the artifact predicted if December quad-witching NDX futures/options settlement volume is being converted into "AUM indexed to the Nasdaq 100." The NDX component also carries the largest single-index standard error in 2021 (1.18 on 3.76, a 31% relative SE) and more than doubled in two years (1.75 → 2.67 → 3.76). Component-level error of this size is invisible in the aggregate 33.5%.

=== FINDING 4. Inference: the reported standard errors are not standard errors for the Russell and Nasdaq components. ===
The paper states plainly (L920-925): "All additions to the Russell 1000 and Russell 2000 occur simultaneously on the last Friday in June each year. For these two indexes, clustering has no effect on our standard errors." That is an admission of one cluster per index-year — so "clustered by announcement" SEs for R1000 (0.51 on 10.77 in 2021) and R2000 (0.03 on 1.06) treat all within-day events as independent draws, which is precisely the assumption that fails: every Russell event in a year shares one day's liquidity conditions, one intermediary inventory state, one index-weight data vintage, and any common recon-day multiplier. The Nasdaq 100 (single annual reconstitution, 17 events in 2021) has the same defect. With one cluster the sampling variance is not identified; the reported figures are within-day dispersion, not standard errors.
The magnitude of the omitted uncertainty is visible in the paper's own time series. Annual changes in the Total column (Table 3) have a standard deviation of 3.55pp and a mean absolute change of 2.67pp, versus a mean reported SE around 1.9pp — the year-to-year swing is ~1.9x the claimed precision. Specific swings: +8.98pp (2007→2008), +6.54pp (2008→2009), −7.53pp (2009→2010), −4.70pp (2014→2015), +3.86pp (2015→2016). The passive share of the US market did not fall by 7.5 percentage points in 2010 and it did not rise 15pp in two years across the crisis. The authors concede the 2009 spike is unexplained and offer two speculations (post-crisis tax-loss harvesting; active managers de-levering). The honest reading is a large year-specific measurement error that the reported SEs do not capture, which means 33.5% is one noisy annual realization, not a measured structural parameter, and the 33.5-vs-16 gap is not established at the precision the paper's t-statistics imply. Appendix B effectively concedes this by fitting a Kalman filter in which "our estimation procedure yields a noisy measurement of the true passive ownership share" — but note that filter uses the ICI index-fund share in its measurement equation (%IndexFundOwned = κ + λ·%Indexed), so the filtered series (34.9% for 2021) is NOT independent corroboration against the ICI benchmark; it is partly constructed from it.

=== FINDING 5. Version drift is far larger than "37.8 → 33.5" implies, and runs the wrong way for the estimator's stability. ===
The 2022 abstract: "passive investors held AT LEAST 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020... based on the CLOSING VOLUMES of index additions and deletions... 37.8% is a lower bound," covering three indexes (S&P 500, Russell 1000, Russell 2000). The JFE version's closing-based 2020 numbers, now across FIVE indexes (Table 4): Volume1600to2359 = 21.37%, VolumeAtClosingPrice = 19.35%, VolumeAtClose = 11.54%. So the same conceptual quantity for the same year fell from 37.8% to somewhere between 11.5% and 21.4% — a 45-70% downward revision — WHILE the index coverage was expanded from three indexes to five (which should push it up). Same for the S&P 500 alone: the 2022 draft's Figure 1 puts strict end-of-day S&P 500 indexers at 22.9% of the market in 2021; JFE Table 3 puts the S&P 500 at 16.80% using the strictly WIDER all-day volume proxy — a >27% downward revision of a single component despite a wider volume window. Two further retreats: the "at least"/"lower bound" framing is dropped in JFE (replaced by an explicit acknowledgment that the estimate may be capturing active volume), and the benchmark drifted from "the widely accepted previous value of 15%" (2020) to 16% (2021). This is a paper whose central number moved by tens of percent between draft and publication as the proxy definition and sample changed, and whose strongest claim (lower bound) did not survive refereeing. An article treating 33.5% as a settled measurement is treating as fixed a number that the authors themselves moved substantially within two years.

=== FINDING 6. The estimator has no null and no baseline subtraction; the headline is the maximum of its own robustness family. ===
Column (1) of Table 4 — the headline — counts 100% of a stock's recon-day volume, including pre-open, all regular-hours, and after-hours trading, as passive rebalancing. There is no specification under which the estimator can return "zero passive ownership": ordinary turnover mechanically converts into implied AUM via Volume x Price / IndexWeight. The only baseline correction offered, column (2) (DailyVolume − ADV), removes 4.85pp in 2021 (33.50 → 28.65) and is itself too small: ADV is measured over the 22 days BEFORE reconstitution, i.e. after the announcement has already elevated the stock's turnover, and on non-witching days for names whose recon day IS a witching day. So even 28.65% under-subtracts. The authors dismiss column (2) with an appeal to a MarketWatch quote ("generally considered the single-biggest trading day in US markets"), not evidence.
Table 6 shows the residuals are not noise but systematically related to observables — %Error is significant in MCap (−0.02, t=2.14), IndexWeight (−0.01, t=4.46), IsAddition (+0.67, t=4.73) and IsMigration (+0.65, t=5.11). The authors dismiss the last two as "economically small" by benchmarking 67bps against the FIVE-INDEX total in the year 2000 (13.4%, "20x smaller") — a category error: the correct denominator is the per-index estimate the error contaminates (e.g. 0.65 on R1000's 10.77 is 6%). The IsMigration coefficient is particularly awkward: the paper elsewhere concedes (L1666, in the elasticity section) that "when a stock gets migrated from, say, the Russell 2000 up to the Russell 1000, some of the buying pressure coming from Russell 1000 investors will be met by Russell 2000 investors who need to sell," and therefore EXCLUDES migrations from the elasticity exercise "to get the cleanest signal" — while migrations remain the workhorse events for the Russell AUM estimates and carry a statistically significant upward bias. Migrations are simultaneously too dirty for elasticities and clean enough for the headline.
Two supporting items on the intermediation channel the paper dismisses ("there is no time to buy from one passive investor and then sell to another"): (a) their own Appendix D shows the trade chain runs through an Authorized Participant who ends the day flat, i.e. the printed volume is an intermediary's print, not the passive investor's; (b) Iro Tasitsiomi, "On the hidden costs of passive investing," arXiv:2506.21775v3 (June 2025, rev. Oct 2025), models exactly this ecosystem and finds liquidity providers profitably accumulate inventory ahead of reconstitution and supply it at the event — a structure in which recon-day prints and passive AUM are related by an intermediation multiplier, not an identity. Tasitsiomi is not a replication or a direct rebuttal, and I do not present it as one; it is an independent modelling of the market microstructure whose implication is that k > 1 is the default, not an exotic possibility.

=== SAMPLE / WINDOW / CONSTRUCT ===
The 2021 headline rests on one year's events from roughly five distinct reconstitution dates: ~38 S&P 500 changes, ~75 direct MidCap changes, 55 R1000 adds, 274 R2000 adds, 17 NDX changes. Pre-2009 Russell weights and all pre-2009 S&P MidCap/Nasdaq weights are INTERPOLATED from monthly/quarterly snapshots, and MidCap weights are never float-adjusted; the authors concede "most of our measurement error seems to be coming from uncertainty about the precise weights" and that it "all but disappears when we have precise index weights directly from the index provider." Since AUM = Volume x Price / Weight, weight error enters inversely and unboundedly — a 10% weight error is a 10% AUM error. This does not damage the 2021 number (direct FTSE data) but it does damage the 2000-2008 half of Figure 2, which is what supports the article's "passive share tripled" arc. Construct validity: the paper is explicit (p.5) that "our procedure counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive holdings; it does not matter who actually owns these assets" — so "passive ownership" here means "dollars whose index-linked slice rebalances at the recon close," which is a broader and softer object than most readers of "passive investors own a third of the market" will assume. Table 5's headline dispersion is also not uniform: 5.49pp average absolute error for the S&P 500 (against a 16.80 point estimate — 33% relative) versus 0.23 for the Russell 2000. The intro's "±1% of each other" is the full-sample average, dominated by the 683-observation Russell 2000; the index contributing half the headline is 24x noisier and never gets its own error reported in the intro.

=== 1. THE HEADLINE NUMBER IS NOT AN ESTIMATE. IT IS A CONSTRUCTED COMPOSITE. ===
The "1/4" is not a coefficient. Sammon multiplies 0.15 by each of four OLS coefficients (Table 2), divides each product by that variable's own whole-sample mean, and takes an EQUAL-WEIGHTED AVERAGE of the four resulting ratios: 0.20 (|Ret|), 0.33 (|Ret|/SD), 0.10 (PJ), 0.29 (IVD) → 0.23 ≈ 1/4. The same four estimates normalized by standard deviations instead give 0.15/0.26/0.08/0.15 → 0.16 ≈ 1/6. So the SAME estimates yield either "one quarter" or "one sixth" purely by choice of denominator, and the paper reports both. The dispersion across the four component ratios is 3.3x (0.10 to 0.33). Reporting a single "~1/4" conceals that the underlying evidence ranges from a tenth to a third depending on which measure you pick.
Compounding this: the four measures are NOT four independent tests. Sammon's own Appendix B.1: |Ret|, |Ret|/SD, and PJ "are functions of what actually occurred on the earnings announcement day." All three are the same announcement-day return with different denominators (nothing, prior-22-day SD, and the T-22..T+2 CAR). Only IVD (options-based) is separately sourced. Averaging four near-collinear ratios as if they were corroborating independent measurements overstates the evidence, and no family-wise correction is applied across them.

=== 2. THE HEADLINE IS OLS, NOT CAUSAL — AND THE FIXED EFFECTS FORBID THE EXTRAPOLATION ===
Sammon's own conclusion: "taking the average of the point estimates from the OLS regressions implies that a 15% increase in passive ownership decreases pre-earnings announcement price informativeness by 1/4th of its whole sample mean." The load-bearing magnitude is the OLS correlation, not the IV.
Equation 4 includes firm fixed effects AND year-quarter fixed effects (φ_t). Year-quarter FE mechanically absorb the entire aggregate time-series path of passive ownership. β is therefore identified purely off WITHIN-quarter, cross-sectional RELATIVE differences in passive ownership across firms. It is then applied to a 30-year AGGREGATE time-series increase in market-wide passive ownership. That counterfactual — "what if aggregate passive ownership had stayed near zero" — is precisely the variation the estimator throws away. This is a partial-equilibrium coefficient being used to price a general-equilibrium change. The relative-vs-aggregate distinction is exactly the fault line in this literature (Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche on demand elasticity; Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg, JFE 145(3), 2022, "On Index Investing," who use the same Russell machinery and find no informativeness effect).
Unit mismatch on top: the 15pp figure is explicitly VALUE-weighted ("value weighted average passive ownership increased by 15%"), while Table 2 columns 1–4 are EQUAL-weighted and Table 1's means are labeled "Cross-sectional equal-weighted means." Equal-weighted passive ownership averages 0.093 in 2010–2019 (p75 = 0.133), i.e. roughly a 10–13pp equal-weighted rise, not 15pp. The internally consistent value-weighted calculation exists (columns 5–6) but is not the one used for the headline, and Sammon declines to report a value-weighted PJ at all because the non-event filter concentrates weight so severely that single firms exceed 10% of a quarter.

Sammon states the maintained assumption as being about SPEED ("earnings announcement news is fully incorporated into prices quickly after its release"). The assumption actually required is about QUANTITY: that the total information content released AT the announcement is orthogonal to passive ownership. That assumption is never stated and never tested.
It is false in his own data. Every figure supporting the causal design (Figure 2, Figures D.8, D.10) plots PASSIVE OWNERSHIP — the treatment — around the event. There is not one event-time plot of |Ret|, |Ret|/SD, PJ, or IVD around index switching. For a causal claim resting entirely on two staggered difference-in-differences designs, the reader is never shown whether the outcome jumped at the event or was already trending.
(c) Russell design. This is NOT a regression discontinuity. It compares firms within ±100 ranks of the threshold that ACTUALLY switched (treated) against those that did not (control) — treatment is selection on having shrunk. Wei Wei & Alex Young, "Selection Bias or Treatment Effect? A Re-Examination of Russell 1000/2000 Index Reconstitution," Critical Finance Review 13(1–2), 2024, 83–115, show that pre-existing differences at the 1000/2000 cutoff mean the common implementation of this setting reflects selection bias rather than treatment effect. Sammon uses the Coles–Heath–Ringgenberg (2022) May market-cap proxy, which is the better of the available reconstructions (99.24% membership prediction), and that earns partial credit — but the switcher-vs-non-switcher DiD is exactly the specification Wei–Young target.
Most damning: the Russell first-stage coefficient on Post × Treated × Passive Gap is 1.77, and Sammon explains the excess over 1 as "there are three years of post-rebalancing observations for the treated firms and the trend toward increased passive ownership has been steeper for Russell 2000 firms than Russell 1000 firms." That is an admission that a large part of the instrument's power comes from a DIFFERENTIAL SECULAR TREND between small and large firms over the three post-years, not from the mechanical index shock. Whatever else differentially trends for small versus large firms over those three years violates the exclusion restriction, and F = 222 provides no protection against that.
(d) S&P 500 design. Committee-selected, as Sammon concedes ("it's possible that the increase in passive ownership is not fully exogenous to firm fundamentals"), and he then documents an increase in post-addition earnings volatility — a direct channel to larger |Ret| that bypasses passive ownership entirely.
(e) Heath et al. reuse correction, misstated. Sammon writes "almost all my IV t-statistics are over 3.62." Computing all eight from Table 3: Russell 4.32 / 4.97 / 2.16 / 4.09; S&P 4.09 / 8.90 / 4.63 / 2.22. Two of eight fall well below his own threshold — PJ in the Russell design (t = 2.16) and IVD in the S&P design (t = 2.22). PJ is the measure he argues is "closest to the measures of price informativeness that arise in a Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) or Kyle (1985)-style model," and it fails the reuse-adjusted bar in one of the two designs. Which two fail is never disclosed.
(f) Staggered adoption, no modern estimator. Overlapping ±3-year windows, cohorts spanning 1990–2019, control firms reused across multiple cohorts, two-way/firm-by-cohort FE. Zero occurrences of "Callaway," "Sun and Abraham," "Goodman-Bacon," "de Chaisemartin," or "staggered." No negative-weighting or heterogeneity-robust check.
(g) IV vs OLS direction. The IV is 2.5–4x the OLS. Sammon reads this as evidence OLS is unbiased. The alternative reading is that the LATE for index switchers is nothing like the population effect being extrapolated to the whole market — which makes the IV useless for validating a headline that is applied market-wide.

=== 6. COMPETING EXPLANATIONS NOT CONTROLLABLE OVER THE PERIOD THAT DRIVES THE RESULT ===
Algorithmic trading. Weller, "Does Algorithmic Trading Reduce Information Acquisition?", Review of Financial Studies 31(6), 2018, 2184–2226, uses the SAME price-jump ratio and finds information in prices falls 9–13% per standard deviation of AT activity, up to a month before scheduled disclosures. AT penetration rose over roughly 1995–2012 — the window that drives Sammon's OLS. His MIDAS AT proxies exist only from 2012, so he CANNOT control for AT over the period generating his result, and on the 2012–2019 window where he can, his |Ret| coefficient is insignificant. Worse, the AT controls behave incoherently in Table C1: Cancel-to-Trade (positively correlated with AT) enters NEGATIVELY on |Ret|, |Ret|/SD, PJ and IVD — i.e. more AT implies MORE pre-announcement informativeness, the opposite of Weller's finding on Weller's own measure. Odd Lot Ratio flips sign across measures. The proxies are evidently picking up liquidity/size, so the "AT is not driving my results" claim is unsupported.
Reg FD (Aug 2000). Sammon's test drops pre-2001 data and calls the result "quantitatively similar." The |Ret| coefficient falls from 0.0635 to 0.0463, a 27% drop from removing one third of the sample — a meaningful attenuation, not similarity. And the test does not address the actual threat, which is a Reg-FD-induced level shift that differs across firms in ways correlated with passive ownership; year-quarter FE absorb the common component only.
Decimalization (2001). ZERO mentions of "decimaliz" or "tick size" in the manuscript. Tick-size reduction is a first-order, well-documented structural break in the profitability of informed pre-announcement trading, hitting in the same year as Reg FD and the same year as the |Ret|/SD acceleration. Not addressed at all.
Insider-trading enforcement. Sammon names it (citing Coffee 2007) as coinciding with the 2001 acceleration, then never tests it.
Four separate structural breaks — Reg FD, decimalization, insider-enforcement, AT — all cluster at the same inflection point he attributes to passive ownership, and none is controllable over the period that generates the estimate.

=== 7. MEASUREMENT AND SAMPLE-SELECTION ===
PJ: the Weller non-event filter deletes 54.5% of announcements, and the deletion is size-correlated (Sammon refuses to value-weight PJ for this reason). N drops from 441,238 to 150,113.
IVD: OptionMetrics begins 1996, and coverage is limited to option-listed equities — under half the sample (112,084 obs). That subsample is skewed toward large, liquid, high-passive firms, so the one genuinely independent measure is estimated on the most selected sample.
Passive ownership: built from CRSP MF + ETF matched via MFLINKS to Thomson S12. Securities never appearing in S12 are IMPUTED AS ZERO passive ownership — a systematic, time-varying error given documented S12 coverage deterioration. Monthly values are LINEARLY INTERPOLATED between quarter-ends, so the pre-announcement passive share partly reflects holdings measured AFTER the announcement (mitigated: he reports results unchanged using last-reported level). The measure also captures only explicitly labeled passive funds, missing internal indexing and closet indexing — Sammon invokes this in footnote 16 to excuse the IV being 3–4x the OLS, i.e. he uses a known measurement failure as an explanation for an anomalous result rather than as a limitation.

=== 8. VERSION DRIFT (four drafts, five years) ===
Apr 2020, "Earnings Announcements and the Rise of Passive Ownership," 1990–2018: three measures — pre-earnings abnormal volume, pre-earnings drift, share of annual volatility on earnings days. No percentage headline. Mechanism: fewer analysts, fewer SEC downloads.
Nov 2021, retitled "Passive Ownership and Price Informativeness," 1990–2018: "three new empirical measures." No percentage headline. Mechanism: "investors expend less effort gathering information."
Mar 2023, 1990–2018: headline "roughly 16%." Mechanism in abstract: less information collection plus limits to arbitrage. Contains a full Section 5 "Mechanisms" with five subsections (5.1 systematic vs idiosyncratic news, 5.2 information gathering, 5.3 sell-side analyst coverage, 5.4 pre-earnings abnormal turnover, 5.5 equilibrium response of non-passive investors).
Oct 2023 = published Management Science version, 1990–2019: headline becomes "approximately 1/4th of its whole sample mean and 1/6th of its whole sample standard deviation." The ENTIRE Section 5 Mechanisms is DELETED, and the mechanism claim is REMOVED from the abstract.
So across drafts the measure set was replaced, the headline grew from 16% to 25% on a one-year sample extension plus a change of normalization, and the evidence for the causal channel was cut. Fragments survive in appendices D.7/D8, but reframed as exclusion-restriction checks — and there, as noted in §3, the analyst/attention results point the WRONG WAY for the mechanism in the S&P experiment. The published paper therefore offers no affirmative mechanism evidence for why passive ownership would cause the effect.

=== AUTHOR INCENTIVES / COI ===
No material conflict found. Sammon is a tenure-track (now associate) professor in the HBS Finance Unit and a CEPR affiliate; the only disclosed financial support in any draft is the Avi Nash Fund (academic). No industry funding, no asset-manager affiliation, no disclosed consulting on the topic. He has since co-authored work that cuts AGAINST simple index-pressure stories (Greenwood & Sammon, "The Disappearing Index Effect," Journal of Finance), which argues against motivated reasoning. The only incentive-relevant observation is structural rather than personal: across drafts the headline number grew and became cleaner while the supporting mechanism evidence was removed — a publication-selection pattern, not a conflict of interest.

=== WHAT SURVIVES ===
The DESCRIPTIVE fact is solid and independently corroborated: over 1990–2019, absolute announcement-day returns rose relative to pre-announcement returns and relative to pre-announcement volatility; |Ret|/SD went from about 1.0 to about 3.5, PJ from about 0.2 to over 0.5. Beaver–McNichols–Wang (JAE 2020) document the same phenomenon with different data and different measures. What does NOT survive is the attribution to passive ownership and the "one quarter of the mean" magnitude.

=== WHY VETO RATHER THAN RESTRICTED_USE ===
Any single one of these would be a RESTRICTED_USE. The combination is disqualifying for load-bearing use, because the failures are not independent — they all point the same way. The confound that the measures cannot exclude (more news at the announcement) is affirmatively PRESENT in the author's own Table D5. The literature that documents that confound as the leading explanation of the same time series is not cited once. And the effect is absent in exactly the recent, high-passive-ownership data where the causal mechanism predicts it should be strongest. A number that is (i) a hand-averaged composite of four collinear ratios, (ii) OLS with the aggregate trend fixed-effected out and then applied to an aggregate trend, (iii) insignificant on the last third of its own sample, (iv) cut roughly in half by three more years of data, and (v) backed by an "almost always insignificant" reduced form with no parallel-trends evidence anywhere, cannot be the strongest pillar of an argument that a price-discovery channel measurably deteriorated because of passive investing. If it is the strongest evidence available, the honest conclusion the article should draw is that the evidence is weak — not that the deterioration is established at one quarter of the mean.

reasoning:
BOTTOM LINE: The 11% figure has NO genuinely independent confirmation (different team AND different data). Every same-direction corroboration I found runs on the same 13F holdings data inside the same Koijen–Yogo demand-system machinery, and in most cases explicitly imports HHL's own decomposition. Meanwhile, two peer-reviewed, fully independent measurements of closely related objects over the same window point the OTHER way, and one of them is a Journal of Finance paper from the same year that HHL never cite. The input to the calculation (the ~32% log drop in active share) is well corroborated; the identifying parameter (pass-through 0.33 / chi = 2.97) is not.

=== WHAT THE CLAIM DECOMPOSES INTO (verified in local extract hhl_main.txt, lines 175-177, 1956-1975) ===
11% = 0.33 pass-through x 32% log drop in active share (broad, elasticity-based measure: active 81.4% -> 59.5% of market cap). HHL's own narrow fund-based measure gives 19% drop -> 6.3%, not 11% (line 1975). Pass-through 0.33 = 1/(1 + chi*|Active|) = 1/(1 + 2.97*0.68).

=== SAME-DIRECTION EVIDENCE — AND WHY NONE OF IT IS INDEPENDENT ===

1. Behmaram, "Indexing and the Elasticity of Stock Demand" (UQAM working paper, v16 dated 1 Apr 2026; SSRN 4823976; local: r3b/behmaram.txt). Different team (solo, UQAM), BUT: same 13F universe, same Koijen–Yogo demand system, and its decomposition is run "following Haddad et al. (2025) equation (29)" (line 2280). This is a within-framework extension, not an independent measurement. Its headline 76% counterfactual is NOT a replication of 11%: it is partial-equilibrium, freezes IXI at the 2000 cross-sectional mean, and the author himself says active offset is only partially netted out (line 2559-2560). Two further problems:
   (a) Its reduced-form analogue of HHL's strategic-response parameter is chi-tilde = 3.9, s.e. 1.7, 95% CI [0.6, 7.3] (line ~2345). Propagating that CI through 1/(1+chi*0.68) x 32% gives an 11% point estimate inside a band of roughly 5%–23%. So the one "independent" read on HHL's key parameter is consistent with the 11% but cannot distinguish it from a third of it or double it.
   (b) Behmaram's two decompositions contradict each other on the very "two-thirds offset" it claims to confirm. The HHL-style accounting decomposition gives a residual absorbing ~65% of the IXI channel (Table 7). But the entity-level Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition finds within-group behavioral change of only −4% to −6%, with composition explaining 103–106% of the total decline (lines 2330-2345) — i.e. active investors barely changed behavior at all, which is closer to a ZERO strategic offset than to two-thirds. Citing Behmaram as confirmation of the two-thirds offset means picking one of his two mutually inconsistent numbers.
   (c) Status: unpublished working paper, not peer reviewed, sole-authored, dated four months before the article's date.

2. van der Beck, Bretscher & Fu, "Rethinking Volume: The Illusion of Liquidity" (HBS WP 26-003, 9 Apr 2026; local: r3b/volume.txt). This is the closest thing to independent same-direction support and it is weak tea. Using the KY demand system on 13F 1980–2025 they find market-cap-weighted long-term price impact "has not materially declined over time. If anything, the market-cap-weighted average impact has slightly increased," and they explicitly call this "consistent with Haddad et al." (lines 1765-1770). But (i) the structural piece again uses 13F + KY, so not independent data/method; (ii) their genuinely independent evidence — net vs gross volume, long-horizon variance ratios, long-run price impact and its reversal from returns/TAQ — delivers a NULL: "long-term liquidity in the U.S. equity market has not meaningfully improved since 1980" (abstract), "the magnitude of the long-run price impact itself appears to have remained stable" (line ~222). A flat line over 45 years is not a positive confirmation of an 11% deterioration; an 11% move is well inside what that series cannot resolve.

3. Chinco & Sammon, "The passive ownership share is double what you think it is" (JFE 2024). Genuinely independent — index-reconstitution-day excess volume, no 13F elasticity classification. HHL themselves cite it (hhl_main.txt line 1823) as corroborating "in a completely different empirical strategy." IMPORTANT: this validates only the INPUT (that true passive ownership is roughly double conventional fund-based estimates, supporting HHL's broad 19%->41% measure over the 6.3% fund-based one). It says nothing about the 0.33 pass-through. So the multiplicand is multi-sourced; the multiplier is not.

4. Pavlova & Sikorskaya, "Benchmarking Intensity" (RFS 36(3), 2023, 859-903). Independent team (LBS), independent data (benchmark mandates/AUM following each index, not 13F elasticity classes). Finds a 1% higher change in BMI -> ~27bp higher return in the reconstitution month. Supports the mechanism (more benchmarked capital -> more price pressure) but is a cross-sectional level estimate, not an aggregate elasticity trend, and cannot be converted into HHL's 11%.

5. Höfler, Schlag & Schmeling, "Passive Investing and Market Quality" (SSRN 4567751). Independent team/data (ETF ownership, option-implied measures, variance decompositions). Finds passive ETF ownership lowers liquidity, raises noise share of returns, strengthens reversals. Same-direction on consequences, but measures market quality, not demand elasticity.

6. Jiang, Vayanos & Zheng, "Passive Investing and the Rise of Mega-Firms" (RFS 38(12), Dec 2025, 3461-3496). Independent, different data (S&P 500 index fund/ETF flows 1996–2020) and method (theory + flow regressions). Passive flows disproportionately raise mega-cap prices and idiosyncratic vol. Mechanism support, no elasticity magnitude.

7. Sabbatucci, Tamoni & Xiao, "Shifting From Active to Passive: How Retirement Plans Impact Equity Prices" (SSRN 4322784). Genuinely different data (BrightScope 401(k) plan-level holdings), same KY demand-system framework. Active->passive transition implies aggregate price changes ~35%; 10% rise in 401(k) demand -> 3.5–4% price rise. Different data, same identification family.

8. Barbon & Gianinazzi, "Quantitative Easing and Equity Prices: Evidence from the ETF Program of the Bank of Japan" (RAPS 9(2), 2019). Fully independent: different country, different data, clean quasi-experiment. Implies long-run elasticity ~1. Confirms demand is inelastic in LEVEL (though ~2-5x more elastic than KY/HHL 13F estimates of 0.2–0.5). Says nothing about a passive-driven trend.

=== OPPOSITE-DIRECTION INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENTS (this is why the verdict is DIRECTION_CONTESTED) ===

9. **Greenwood & Sammon, "The Disappearing Index Effect," Journal of Finance 80(2), April 2025, 657-698** (local: r3b/gs_hbs.txt). Same publication year and same tier as HHL. Fully independent: different team, different data (S&P 500 addition/deletion event returns plus measured index-tracker demand shocks, 1980s–2020), different identification (event study, no demand system, no 13F elasticity classification). Result, verbatim from the text: the multiplier M "has fallen by a factor of roughly 20, from 6.75 in the late 1990s to 0.37 in the last decade," and for deletions "from 10.76 in the late 1990s to 0.7." Converting, implied elasticity moved from −0.09/−0.15 in the 1990s to −0.28/−0.17 in the 2000s to −1.44/−2.72 in the 2010s (lines 695-715). That is demand becoming roughly an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE MORE ELASTIC across precisely HHL's 2001–2020 window, while indexation grew — the opposite sign of trend, and 100x the magnitude of HHL's 11%. It survives the authors' own robustness checks: accounting for index migrations (which shrink the measured demand shock) still leaves a factor-20 fall, and using a 20-day pre-announcement window (allowing for anticipation) still leaves a factor-7 fall (lines 700-735). Their interpretation is explicitly that active institutions absorb the passive demand: "although index trackers now buy about 7-8% upon index addition, total institutional ownership barely moves around index changes. We interpret this as professional active investors providing liquidity to passive buyers and sellers" (line ~130) — i.e. an offset far exceeding HHL's two-thirds. **HHL do not cite Greenwood & Sammon anywhere in the main text or appendix** (I grepped both: hits are only for Greenwood-Vayanos on bonds and Sammon's separate informativeness/reconstitution papers). The two flagship 2025 results on this question are pointed in opposite directions and are not reconciled in print.
   Rebuttal that exists: van der Beck, Bretscher & Fu (volume.txt, footnote 3) argue the disappearing index effect "may reflect intertemporal shifting of price pressure — due to anticipation and front-running — rather than a reduction in aggregate price impact." So G&S is contested, not decisive. But it is contested by a working paper, not settled.
   Note also a direct head-to-head contradiction inside the passive literature: Behmaram claims S&P 500 additions cause a 3.5pp IXI jump and a 12% DECLINE in the added stock's elasticity (line 3158), while Greenwood & Sammon measure the price impact of the identical event falling ~20-fold. Same event, opposite conclusions, different methods.

10. **Koijen & Yogo, "An Equilibrium Model of Institutional Demand and Asset Prices," JF 74(4) 2019** — the parent framework HHL build on, different team. Their own time series over 1980–2014 reports that "price impact for the average institution has decreased from 1980 to 2014, especially for [the least liquid stocks]" and that "the cross-sectional distribution of price impact has significantly compressed over this period" (lines 96-101, 1197-1199 of the extracted text). At the type level the trend is mixed, not monotone: "banks, insurance companies, and pension funds have become less elastic from 1980 to 2014, while investment advisors and households have become more elastic" (line 1085-1087). The framework's own long-run time series does not display the clean inelasticity drift the 11% narrative implies; HHL's result comes from a different aggregation and a shorter window.

11. **Chaudhry & Li, "Endogenous Elasticities: Price Multipliers Are Smaller for Larger Demand Shocks" (SSRN 5325371, June 2025; Fisher WP 2025-03-15).** Independent team, different data (measured demand shocks, not structural KY). Finds stock-level multipliers are smaller for larger contemporaneous AND larger cumulative past shocks — investors become endogenously more elastic as dislocations grow, so "large shocks expand rather than exhaust the capacity of markets to absorb shocks." This directly attacks the extrapolation step: HHL apply a locally-estimated linear pass-through to a 20-year, 32%-of-market cumulative reallocation. If elasticity is endogenous in shock size, 11% is an upper bound, and the true effect is smaller.

12. **Yicheng Wang, "Estimating Investor Demand Elasticity with Endogenous Firm Responses" (Minnesota, July 2025; AFA program).** Independent team, different data (mutual fund flow shocks + equity issuance), different method (indirect inference on a dynamic structural model). Finds residual-investor elasticity of 2.4 versus ~0.73 from the naive pooled approach — a 3x level correction — because firms respond to price pressure by issuing equity, and concludes "strategic interactions cause marginal price effects to diminish rapidly with the size of demand shocks." Cites HHL (line 152) as finding "weaker-than-expected strategic reactions." Same direction of attack as Chaudhry–Li.

13. **van der Beck, "Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing," JFE 2026** (published: ScienceDirect S0304405X2600108X; local: r3b/vdb.txt). Long-run elasticities are ~4x quarterly; AUM-weighted long-run elasticity 1.45; price impacts ~3x larger at quarterly horizons than in long-run equilibrium (lines 64, 126-129, 1066). This is a construct-validity challenge: HHL's object is a horizon-ambiguous holdings-based elasticity, and "how prices respond to trading" in an article about markets being broken is naturally a persistent-horizon question. Complication worth flagging: van der Beck's own later co-authored paper (item 2) argues that coefficients identified from holdings IN LEVELS correspond to LONG-run elasticities — so the two van der Beck papers are not fully aligned on which horizon HHL's number lives at.

Several read the identical reallocation of return variance into the announcement window as markets getting BETTER, not worse. That is a genuine direction contest on the claim the article is leaning on.

=== A. GENUINELY INDEPENDENT SAME-DIRECTION MEASUREMENTS (mechanism claim) ===

A1. Höfler, Schlag & Schmeling, "Passive Investing and Market Quality" (working paper, March 2025 version; AFA 2025, SFS Cavalcade 2024; Goethe Univ. Frankfurt / SAFE / CEPR). Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/hss.txt. Fully independent team, different measure family (Brogaard, Nguyen, Putniņš & Wu (2022) return-variance decomposition), overlapping-but-differently-implemented identification (Russell 2000 assignment IV with Appel-Gormley-Keim banding controls), data 2000-2020 (extends one year past Sammon). Per SD of passive ETF ownership (Table IA, bandwidth 300, N=17,193): FirmInfo variance share −8.01 (t=−2.82); PrivateInfo share −10.2 (t=−3.42); Noise share +6.09 (t=3.88); MktInfo +1.93 (t=0.76, insig.); PublicInfo +2.18 (t=0.90, insig.). Alternative horizon spec: PrivateInfo −13.73 (t=−4.10). This is the single strongest independent confirmation available, because "PrivateInfo share falls, MktInfo unchanged" is precisely Sammon's proposed channel (passive owners collect less firm-specific information) measured without any earnings-announcement window at all.

A2. Bennett, Stulz & Wang, "Does Joining the S&P 500 Index Hurt Firms?" (NBER w27593, 2020; published JFE). Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/bsw.txt. Independent team, 1997-2017, S&P 500 additions with matched controls, firm+year FE, firm-clustered SEs. Two measures, neither earnings-based: Rsq (market-model R²) and GPIN (Duarte-Hu-Young generalized PIN). Panel A: SP500Add → Rsq +0.022 (t=2.81); GPIN −0.021 (t=−3.95). Panel B regresses informativeness directly on passive holdings: no link for Rsq, strong negative link for GPIN. Sammon himself benchmarks against this (his §"comparison with the literature"): a 24% passive-ownership increase → GPIN decline of ~0.09 vs GPIN mean 0.07 / SD 0.17 — i.e., BSW's implied effect is LARGER than Sammon's, "same order of magnitude."
IMPORTANT CAVEAT I found in BSW that Sammon does not surface: BSW's GPIN effect "decreases significantly less in the late period" (Late = 2008+), which they call "a weaker treatment effect of index addition on price informativeness." The attenuation is in exactly the sub-period when passive ownership grew fastest — a time-series pattern in tension with Sammon's "rise in passive over 30 years caused the decline" extrapolation. BSW also find no effect of index addition on investment efficiency in the late period.

A3. Israeli, Lee & Sridharan, "Is there a dark side to exchange traded funds? An information perspective," Review of Accounting Studies 22(3), 2017, 1048-1083. Independent team, ETF-ownership panel, four outcomes: higher bid-ask spreads, higher return synchronicity, LOWER future earnings response coefficients (FERC), fewer analysts. The FERC result is the closest independent analogue to Sammon's construct — FERC literally measures the degree to which today's price already impounds future earnings, i.e. pre-announcement anticipation — and it moves the same way. Sammon distinguishes himself from ILS (his fn.2) by saying ILS study the "contemporaneous relationship... conditional on a given amount of information being released," but the FERC test is not contemporaneous and does corroborate him.

A4. Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg, "On index investing," JFE 145(3), 2022 — PARTIAL/upstream confirmation only. Independent team, Russell RDD. They confirm the INPUT channel: Google search volume −3.8%, EDGAR page views −14.1%, analyst reports −10.8% with more index investing. But see C1 — their price-side result is a null.

=== B. INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF THE DESCRIPTIVE TREND, WITH A NON-PASSIVE ATTRIBUTION ===

B1. Martineau, "Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift," Critical Finance Review (accepted; Univ. of Toronto), sample 1984-2019. Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/martineau.txt. This is the most consequential thing I found. Martineau independently documents that "pre-announcement drifts have also significantly weakened over time" — Sammon's core descriptive fact, from a different team with a different research question — AND that announcement-day price response is 6x (all-but-microcap) and 3x (microcap) more responsive to earnings surprises in 2016-2019 than in 1984-1990, with PEAD gone since 2006 for all-but-microcap and announcement-date prices now a martingale w.r.t. one-quarter-ahead prices. He explicitly tests and rejects the pre-announcement channel as the explanation: "A weakening in pre-announcement drifts does not explain the improvement in the response of announcement date returns to earnings surprises." His conclusion is the opposite welfare sign from Sammon's: "stock prices have become more efficient following earnings announcements." Same reallocation of price discovery into the announcement window; passive investing is not part of his explanation at all.

B2. Beaver, McNichols & Wang, "Increased market response to earnings announcements in the 21st century: An empirical investigation," Journal of Accounting and Economics 69(1), 2020, sample 2001-2016. Independent team documenting the rise in announcement-day return variability and volume — the same trend that drives Sammon's |Ret| series — and attributing a substantial fraction of it to CONCURRENT information bundled INTO the announcement: management guidance, disaggregated financial-statement line items, and analyst forecasts released at the announcement. Their diagnostic is decisive: market response to guidance issued SEPARATELY from earnings DECLINED over the same period, while bundled guidance rose. That is a passive-free, mechanically-evidenced alternative generator of Sammon's headline trend. Sammon does not cite this paper anywhere in the October 2023 draft (I grepped; no Beaver citation).

B3. Weller, "Does Algorithmic Trading Reduce Information Acquisition?" RFS 31(6), 2018, 2184-2226; 54,879 stock-quarters of SEC MIDAS data. Same PJ price-jump measure Sammon adopts. Information in prices falls 9-13% per SD of algorithmic-trading activity, "up to a month before scheduled disclosures." Independent team, different data, same measure, same direction on the outcome — but a competing attribution. Sammon addresses this (App. C.2.2) by adding Weller's four AT proxies as controls, coefficients survive; but MIDAS starts in 2012, so the AT control is available for only 8 of his 30 years and cannot speak to the 1990-2012 trend that carries most of his time-series identification.

=== C. GENUINELY INDEPENDENT OPPOSITE-DIRECTION / NULL MEASUREMENTS ===

C1. Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (JFE 2022), price side. Russell reconstitution RDD — the SAME instrument family as Sammon's first IV, and Sammon explicitly follows their sample-construction procedure (he cites Coles et al. 2022 six times for method). They find NO effect across "a range of measures of price informativeness, including anomaly mispricing and post-earnings announcement drift," and characterize their tests as well-powered. Their conclusion: "the fraction and effort of informed investors adjust so that the relation between price and fundamental value is unchanged." That is a direct null on the outcome using the same identification, from the team whose methodology Sammon borrows. Sammon lists them as the one paper finding "no relationship" and moves on.

C2. Hu & Liang, "Passive Institutional Ownership and the Informational Efficiency of Stock Prices," Journal of Accounting, Auditing & Finance, published online 23 March 2026 (DOI 10.1177/0148558X261435231). Independent team, identification = S&P 500 additions — Sammon's SECOND IV. They ACCEPT that passive reduces pre-announcement informativeness and then show, on the same shock, that passive → greater firm disclosure, HIGHER earnings response coefficients, and WEAKER PEAD. Their synthesis is explicitly the opposite reading of Sammon's own configuration: less pre-announcement leakage + more complete incorporation at the announcement + less drift = better information environment. This is the sharpest available demonstration that Sammon's measured facts do not pin down his sign.

C3. Glosten, Nallareddy & Zou, "ETF Activity and Informational Efficiency of Underlying Securities," Management Science 67(1), 2021, 22-47. Independent team. ETF trading INCREASES informational efficiency, "resulting from the timely incorporation of systematic earnings information," concentrated in stocks with weak information environments and imperfectly competitive markets. Note the interpretive collision: Sammon cites GNZ as roughly corroborating him ("going from bottom to top decile of ETF ownership increases earnings response by 0.11 vs. average 0.240... similar magnitude to my estimate"), but GNZ read that same increased earnings response as efficiency IMPROVING. Identical coefficient, opposite welfare sign. HSS's decomposition arbitrates partly in GNZ's favor: MktInfo share is unchanged/positive while only PrivateInfo falls.

C4. Choi, "The Conditional Price Efficiency of Passive Investing" (SSRN 5480703, April 2026) and the related "Complementarity of Passive and Active Investment on Stock Price Efficiency." Independent author, Russell reconstitution IV — again Sammon's own instrument. Finds instrumented passive increases produce "economically large improvements in price efficiency" in firms with substantial active mutual-fund ownership, and negligible effects where active ownership is thin. Since passive ownership is highest in large caps, which are also the most actively covered, this cuts against extrapolating Sammon's average effect to the market-cap-weighted market.

C5. Kacperczyk, Sundaresan & Wang, "Do Foreign Institutional Investors Improve Price Efficiency?" RFS 34(3), 2021, 1317-1367 (NBER w24765, 2018 — this is the "Kacperczyk et al. (2018b)" Sammon rebuts in his fn.8). Local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/ksw.txt. International panel 2000-2013, MSCI additions + JGTRRA as ownership shocks. VERSION-DRIFT FINDING: Sammon's rebuttal quotes PJ coefficients (MSCI −0.041, JGTRRA −0.225 on Weller's price-jump measure) from that paper, but I could not locate the Weller PJ measure in either the 2018 NBER working paper or the published RFS article — neither contains the string "Weller" or "price jump." The published paper's primary measure is the Bai-Philippon-Savov predicted-cash-flow-variation PI, with PEAD as a robustness check. So the opposite-signed PJ estimate Sammon argues against appears to have been dropped between drafts, and the surviving published result on passive is a NULL: "the effects for passive ownership are largely insignificant" (their §5.1, three-year horizon; passive there = index funds/ETFs plus pension funds, banks, insurers, a broader construct than Sammon's). Anyone repeating Sammon's fn.8 should not cite it as a live opposite-sign result, and anyone citing KSW against Sammon should say "null," not "opposite."

C6. Kacperczyk, Nosal & Sundaresan, "Market Power and Price Informativeness," Review of Economic Studies 92(3), May 2025 (local copy: .../scratchpad/r3c/kns.txt, July 2024 version). This is now a pure THEORY paper — no PJ empirics survive. Its model prediction is mixed for Sammon: informativeness is decreasing in the size of the passive sector (supports him) but non-monotonic in oligopolist size and decreasing in concentration (a competing driver over the same 30 years, since ownership concentration rose sharply alongside passive). Their dominant channel is information pass-through, not learning.

C7. Bai, Philippon & Savov, "Have financial markets become more informative?" JFE 122(3), 2016, 625-654. Independent team, 1960-2014, welfare-based measure (predicted variation of future cash flows from prices). Informativeness ROSE at 3-5 year horizons, and the rise is "concentrated among firms with greater institutional ownership and share turnover, firms with options trading, and growth firms" — i.e., concentrated where passive ownership is highest. Sammon acknowledges this (his fn.6) and argues compatibility via a Campbell-Shiller decomposition. The reconciliation is coherent but it is his own, not independently tested, and it means the two literatures never meet on a common measure.

C8. Farboodi, Matray, Veldkamp & Venkateswaran, "Where Has All the Data Gone?" RFS 35(7), 2022, 3101-3138 (lead article). Independent team. Large growth-firm prices increasingly reflect future earnings; small and value firms flat or declining. The cross-sectional gradient runs the WRONG way for Sammon's mechanism: passive ownership is most concentrated in exactly the large-cap firms whose prices became MORE informative about future fundamentals. Sammon does not cite this paper (grepped; no Farboodi citation in the Oct-2023 draft). It is arguably the sharpest cross-sectional contradiction available and it went unaddressed.

C9. López Vilaró, "Index Fund Ownership and Stock Price Efficiency: Evidence from Quarterly Earnings Seasons" (Univ. of Arkansas dissertation, 2023). On-point but low-weight: finds competing effects (lower investor disagreement around announcements = better; reduced peer-information incorporation = worse) and concludes "no conclusive evidence on the total impact of index fund ownership at currently observed levels."

=== D. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE ARTICLE ===
The article's framing — "the strongest evidence that SOME price-discovery channel measurably deteriorated" — survives only in its narrowest form. Defensible: the private/firm-specific-information share of price formation declines with passive ownership, confirmed by three independent teams on three different measures (HSS variance decomposition, BSW GPIN, ILS FERC). Not defensible: presenting Sammon's pre-announcement result as a clean, corroborated deterioration finding. Two independent teams running Sammon's own instruments (CHR on Russell, Hu-Liang on S&P 500 additions, plus Choi on Russell) get null or improvement; two independent teams (Martineau, Beaver et al.) reproduce his descriptive trend and attribute it to faster announcement-day processing and to more information being bundled into announcements; and the paper GNZ that Sammon counts in his favor reads its own coefficient as an efficiency gain.

=== MEASUREMENTS THAT LAND LOWER (magnitude tension, NOT direction contradiction) ===

(6) Pavlova & Sikorskaya, "Benchmarking Intensity," Review of Financial Studies 36(3), 2023, 859-903 (LBS). Holdings-based stock-level BMI; mean BMI ~0.159 in matched samples. Their own text concedes they lack data "for assets of benchmarked investors other than mutual funds and ETFs."

(7) Behmaram, "Indexing and the Elasticity of Stock Demand," April 2026 working paper. Indexing Inclusion Ratio (IXI): realized passive ownership from >17,000 funds' actual holdings across >570 benchmarks, adjusted for Active Share. Average IXI 13.4% in 2022-2023; unadjusted IXI_non-adj ~17%; BMI ~15.9%. He cites C&S approvingly ("actual passive ownership is approximately double self-declared index fund holdings") rather than contesting it, and his universe is fund holdings only.

(8) Bloomberg Intelligence (Seyffart 2023, as cited by C&S): "at least 19%" — above ICI's 16%, far below 33.5%.

WHY THESE DO NOT MAKE THIS DIRECTION_CONTESTED: (6), (7) and (8) all measure only the FUND universe — precisely the universe C&S argue is incomplete — so by construction they cannot rebut the claim that money outside that universe exists. But they carry a real cautionary signal for the article: every measurement that demands holdings-level documentation tops out around 13-17%; the gap between that and 33.5% is not observed in ANY holdings dataset. It is inferred from volume (C&S), from price elasticity (HHL), from survey self-report (S&P DJI, BlackRock), or from transaction records in a foreign market (Escobar et al.) — never from US holdings data. That is worth saying out loud in the article.

=== VERSION-DRIFT NOTE (relevant to how much weight the level can bear) ===
The 2022 working paper (local cs_2022.txt) headline: "passive investors held at least 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020." The published JFE Table 3 gives 32.19% (SE 2.91) for 2020. The same year's estimate fell 5.6pp — roughly 2 standard errors — between working paper and publication. The article should quote only the published 33.5% (2021), never 37.8%.

=== CONCLUSION ===
UPGRADE_MULTISOURCE. Escobar-Pandolfi-Pedraza-Williams (2026) is the decisive addition: a different team, a different country, a different index family, and transaction-level investor identities rather than volume inference, independently finding that undeclared benchmarked money generates 1.7x the rebalancing demand of declared index funds (2.7x total multiplier). Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche (AER 2025) independently put US passive at 41% by 2020 via a demand system. BlackRock's own 2017 accounting implies a 2.36x multiplier. S&P DJI's survey shows one index family alone accounts for ~20% of US market cap in indexed assets. Nothing anywhere points the other way. The claim's DIRECTION is now well multi-sourced; the specific 33.5% figure is not, and should be attributed rather than stated as settled fact.
